A lemniscate is a figure-eight or infinity-shaped curve defined as the locus of points whose product of distances to two fixed foci equals a constant. The name comes from the Latin word for ribbon. It stands as one of the most elegant algebraic curves, combining visual symmetry with remarkable mathematical properties. The lemniscate of Bernoulli is the most famous type. Its Cartesian equation is x squared plus y squared all squared equals a squared times x squared minus y squared, where two a is the distance between the two foci. The polar equation is r squared equals a squared cosine two theta, which reveals the figure-eight shape more compactly. The lemniscate has two loops, one on each side, that meet at a central point at the origin, forming its characteristic infinity shape. The curve has a special property: the product of distances from any point on the lemniscate to the two foci is constant and equals a squared over two. The area of one loop equals a squared, and the total area of both loops is two a squared. Jacob Bernoulli, of the famous Bernoulli family of mathematicians, first studied the lemniscate in sixteen ninety-four as a variation on the ellipse. The lemniscate's visual form inspired the mathematical symbol for infinity, the sideways eight, which visually resembles the curve's two-looped form.
